submitted.rationale: Index 3 (Ni 0.24) gave the highest photocurrent of the three measured, 2.07 µA. Photocurrent rises steadily as the V fraction increases: 0.38 µA at Ni 0.53, 1.42 µA at Ni 0.34 and 2.07 µA at Ni 0.24. This points to a V-rich vanadate or V2O5 mixture as the best absorber at 3.22 eV.

rejected.reason: Measured 0.38 µA. The Ni2V2O7 region is much weaker.
Measured 1.42 µA at the NiV2O6 stoichiometry, below index 3.
Photocurrent falls as Ni increases, and NiO-like phases tend to be p-type. Not measured because the merit budget was used up.

consultations.verdict: Support: NiV2O6 (Ni 0.333) is near-hull (0.05 eV/atom) with HSE gap 2.5 eV, below the 3.22 eV photons, so it is a plausible absorbing n-type vanadate. Index 12 (Ni 0.34) sits at this stoichiometry. Ni-richer vanadates have smaller gaps but are less stable and trend toward p-type NiO.

Mixed. The V-rich Ni2V8O15 is well off-hull (0.19 eV/atom) and has a metallic-like small gap of 0.9 eV. That argues against the V-rich end as a well-defined semiconductor. So I'm probing the Ni2V2O7 side instead (index 9, Ni 0.53). Earlier receipts put Ni2V2O7 at an HSE gap of 1.86 eV, which absorbs strongly at 3.22 eV.

Weakly against. The NiV3O6 hypothetical phase has a small gap of 0.77 eV and would be a poor photoanode, but a real film at Ni 0.24 is probably V2O5 mixed with NiV2O6. The data show photocurrent dropping as Ni increases (1.42 µA at Ni 0.34 vs 0.38 µA at Ni 0.53), and the GP UCB picks index 3. So I'll use the last measurement to test the V-rich side.
